name: Scottish independence
summary: Scottish independence is the political movement for Scotland to leave the United Kingdom and govern itself as a sovereign state, within the European Union in the SNP's version. Its mainstream, the SNP's, sees devolution as a step toward independence and pursues it by referendum, with a left-of-centre programme.
scope: The modern political movement for Scotland to become an independent state, as the scholarship and reference works on it describe it (Keating's 'independentist' tradition, which Keating dates from the 1930s and sees becoming a serious option in the 1970s with the SNP; Britannica's account of the SNP's aim). Its programme is taken in the form the SNP and the Scottish Government gave it: independence by referendum (the 2012 Edinburgh Agreement, the 2013 white paper Scotland's Future, the post-2016 demand for a second referendum), in the EU, with the movement's own account of what independence is for. Excludes the medieval Wars of Scottish Independence (the subject of Maxwell's 1909 Robert the Bruce book) and Hugh King's 1914 history of feudalism in Scotland: they concern the medieval kingdom's independence and land law, and neither the scholarship nor the SNP ties them to the modern movement's tenets, so they are not cited. Also excludes the wider Scottish nationalism (its own catalog entry), Scottish republicanism, and devolution or 'home rule' as such, which the sources distinguish from the independentist tradition.

keyFigures.quote: Nicola Sturgeon: Sturgeon succeeded Salmond as first minister and SNP leader. She led the SNP to an unprecedented showing in the 2015 UK general election, where the party won 56 of the 59 Scottish seats in the British Parliament.

common-currency.rationale: Keating says the SNP and the Scottish Government adopted a plan to share the pound sterling in a monetary union with the rest of the UK, though the Greens and the left of the movement did not; this is a position on one currency union, held with dissent.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Keating (section on the campaign) says the Yes side projected a modern, civic notion of Scottish identity shorn of ethnic particularism, so it did not define the nation by one ethnic group.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Keating (section "Defence and Security") reports that the SNP's independence plans were for a nuclear-free Scotland, with the UK deterrent removed; an independent Scotland was not to hold nuclear weapons.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Keating reports Salmond's proposal that an independent Scotland keep the monarchical union, among five of six unions retained; this accepts a hereditary monarch as head of state.

national-resource-control.rationale: The SNP's Constitution page presents Westminster control over Scotland's energy as the cause of high prices, and Keating reports the Yes side's claim to Scotland's North Sea oil revenues; both are about Scotland's own resources.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Keating (section "Defence and Security") reports that SNP policy is that Scotland should be nuclear-free, so Trident would have to be withdrawn from Scotland.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Britannica says the SNP seeks an independent state within the European Union; Keating says the SNP has used Europe as an essential external support for independence since the late 1980s and was the UK's most pro-European party; Anderson and Keil say it advocated continued EU membership.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Keating (section on the campaign) says the Yes side embraced immigration and multiculturalism; tight restriction is the opposite of that stated stance.

right-to-secede.rationale: Keating treats the right to self-determination as the issue settled by the Edinburgh Agreement, and the BBC reports Sturgeon calling the Supreme Court ruling "democracy denial" and seeking a lawful route for Scots to express their will; the sources state this for Scotland, not for regions in general.
